blindSummary:
A 2024 criminal conversion-practices ban (bipartisan, in force from April 2025) makes practices directed at changing or suppressing sexual orientation or gender identity criminal offences punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, including taking a person to another state/province or abroad for the purpose or engaging a provider outside the state/province. A civil complaints scheme runs through the state/province's anti-discrimination body. This state/province also operates an explicit self-identification prison-placement policy, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

Against these strong legal protections, it carries a concentrated violence pattern. A trans woman was killed in her apartment (January 2020); the accused admitted killing her after learning she was transgender and the case went to murder trial in a state high court - a positive institutional response. A 25-year-old trans woman who had arrived in the country approximately six weeks earlier was strangled; her killer received only 22 months on a consensual-strangulation account that public-broadcaster reporting showed the court never heard contested. Two killings of trans women in the same state/province within roughly a year, with one adequate and one clearly inadequate sentencing outcome, is recorded as a pattern plus a contested institutional response, not as isolated incidents. The state/province follows the common law, with no statutory bill of rights and no state/provincial anti-vilification offence comparable to a neighbouring state/province's 2025 criminal provision.

Against the country-wide baseline, this state/province sits slightly below it: the criminal conversion-practice ban and self-identification custody are strong positives but narrow in direct traveler-facing exposure (a typical tourist is unlikely to encounter a conversion-practice provider), while the violence-and-sentencing pattern is more relevant to a visitor's physical safety and shows both institutional capability (the murder trial) and institutional failure (the 22-month sentence). Compared with a neighbouring state/province, which has the criminal vilification offence this one lacks, the two trade different kinds of protection.
